يَدَيْهِ:
Meaning *"his two hands"*, it comes from *يَد (yad)*, meaning *hand*, in the dual form with the suffix *-hi*, referring to two hands belonging to someone.

In Qur'anic Arabic, it often appears in expressions with broader meanings. The phrase *بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ (bayna yadayhi)*, literally *"between his two hands"*, is a common idiom meaning *before him*, *in front of him*, or *that which already precedes him*. Accordingly, when the Qur'an speaks of confirming *مَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ*, classical commentators understood it as referring to earlier scriptures already present at the time.
أَعْقَابِكُمْ:
Meaning *"your heels"*, it is the plural of *عَقِب (ʿaqib)*, meaning *heel* or *the back part of the foot*. In classical Arabic, turning back on one's heels became an idiom for retreating, reversing course, or abandoning one's previous path.

Accordingly, the expression *يَرُدُّوكُمْ عَلَىٰ أَعْقَابِكُمْ* in Qur'an 3:149 means *"they will turn you back on your heels"*, not merely in a physical sense but by causing believers to abandon their faith. The verse continues with *فَتَنقَلِبُوا خَاسِرِينَ* (*"and you would become losers"*), showing that the 'turning back' refers to spiritual and religious regression rather than simply walking backward.

The same imagery appears elsewhere in the Qur'an, such as *انقلب على عقبيه* (*turned back on his two heels*), describing apostasy, retreat from faith, or reversal after guidance.
